t: Minimum Total Price After Applying Discounts
o: We must pair at most min(len(prices), len(discounts)) discounts to items, one-to-one, minimizing the total final price — equivalently maximizing total saved amount p·d/100. In Example 1, pairing 60% with 30 and 50% with 21 saves 18 + 10.5 = 28.5 from a base of 61, giving 32.5. Example 3 shows leftover items simply stay undiscounted. With arrays up to 10⁵, exponential assignment is impossible; the classic rearrangement-inequality argument says sorting both arrays and pairing in the same order is optimal.
k: Minimizing final price = maximizing total savings sum(p_i * d_j)/100.
By the rearrangement inequality, the maximum sum of products pairs the largest prices with the largest discounts.
Only the first min(n, m) pairs are used; extras on either side are ignored.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force over Permutations (small inputs)
a.i: Try every way of choosing which items get which discounts and take the minimum. Only viable for tiny inputs; included to establish the baseline.
s: Enumerate injections from discounts to item indices.
Sum final prices for each assignment.
a.t: Exponential, O(C(n,k) · (n + k)) — only for tiny inputs.

a.n: Approach 2: Sort Both and Pair Greedily (Optimal)
a.i: Savings are products p·d. By the rearrangement inequality, the sum of products is maximized when both sequences are sorted the same way. So sort prices descending and discounts descending, pair positionally, and add the discounted prices for those pairs plus untouched prices otherwise.
s: Sort prices descending and discounts descending.
For i < min(n, m), add prices[i]*(100-discounts[i])/100.
Add remaining unpaired prices; return the total.
a.t: O(n log n + m log m) — sorting dominates; the pairing scan is linear.
a.sp: O(1) extra (in-place sort), or O(n) in Java due to boxing.

w: Always present the rearrangement-inequality argument — interviewers want proof the greedy pairing is optimal, not just intuition. Pitfalls: floating-point precision (use doubles; answers within 1e-5 accepted), handling more discounts than items and vice versa, and remembering an unmatched discount is simply wasted. Follow-ups: what if each discount could be reused, or each item could take multiple discounts?
